questions.subject: FRENCH
questions.topic: Royal officers in the Capetian kingdom
questions.learningObjective: explain how royal administration was extended in the Capetian kingdom
questions.stem: In the Capetian kingdom the king sends officers drawn from his own household into the counties to collect dues and hold justice in his name. What is the point of the arrangement?

options.text: The officers are royal appointees, so the king's authority runs through them and not through a local lord
The officers are chosen by the local barons, who appoint one of their number to watch the king
options.misconception: makes the king's agents into local nobles, which is the opposite of the arrangement described

options.text: The officers are churchmen, since the Crown handed its jurisdiction to the bishop of each county
options.misconception: hands judicial authority to the Church, which the royal officers were there to displace

options.text: The officers are tax farmers who paid for the right to gather dues and kept what they collected
options.misconception: confuses a paid office of the Crown with a private purchase of the right to tax

questions.explanation: From the eleventh century onwards the Capetian kings sent baillis and sénéchaux, drawn from the royal household, to administer the royal domain and to extend the king's justice beyond the territory he owned outright. The trap is confusing royal officers with seigneurial bailiffs, whose authority came from the lord they served.

questions.topic: Reading a medieval charter
questions.learningObjective: identify a charter from its content and its binding force
questions.stem: A medieval document records that a town has received the right to hold its own market and to be spared a certain tax. What kind of text is it?

options.text: A charter, which registers privileges granted to a town and binding on whoever granted them
A chronicle, which records a king's deeds so that later kings can copy what he did
options.misconception: reads a grant as a narrative, where a chronicle reports rather than confers

options.text: A sermon, which sets out in Latin what the local clergy expected of the parish
options.misconception: takes a document in Latin to be a text of preaching rather than of law

options.text: A trial record, which preserves the words of witnesses in a dispute about land
options.misconception: confuses a recorded concession with the deposition of witnesses in court

questions.explanation: A « charte » or « octroi de coutumes » states what a lord or a king grants: a market, a toll exemption, freedom from a service, the right to elect judges. The trap is filing a grant among narratives; a chronicle tells a reader what happened, a charter tells everyone what will hold.
questions.hint: Ask whether the text describes an event or creates an obligation.

questions.topic: The Concordat of 1801
questions.learningObjective: state what the Concordat settled between state and church
questions.stem: In 1801 an agreement settles how bishops are appointed and how the Church is paid for, and it holds for most of the following century. What is the agreement?

The Pragmatic Sanction, which gave the Church the right to elect its bishops with no state role at all
options.misconception: names a text that regulated rather than separated the two, and dates it correctly enough

options.text: A private treaty between two families, which settled a succession and was never a state matter
options.misconception: confuses an arrangement about appointment with one that abolished the state's role entirely

options.text: A sentence of excommunication, which placed the king outside the Church until he recanted
options.misconception: reads a private agreement as a matter of dynasty rather than of public law

questions.topic: Who paid for the French Renaissance
questions.learningObjective: identify the patronage behind French Renaissance culture
questions.stem: A sixteenth-century French king invites Italian painters to his court and pays for their work out of his own household. What does that show about French Renaissance culture?

options.text: That court and aristocratic patronage paid for it, and that royal collecting brought foreign artists in
That the Church refused all patronage, so the movement grew entirely outside religious circles

options.text: That it was a purely popular art paid for by the people and unknown to the courts of Europe
options.misconception: turns court art into a movement with no patrons at all, which no art history supports

options.text: That printing rather than money produced the paintings, since a copy was the only way to get one
options.misconception: confuses the spread of engravings with the commissioning of the original work

questions.topic: The Edict of Nantes and its revocation
questions.learningObjective: state what the Edict of Nantes granted and how it ended
questions.stem: A settlement of 1598 gave Huguenots a limited freedom of worship in certain places, and it was revoked in 1685. What is the settlement, and what ended it?

options.text: The Edict of Nantes, which ended the religious wars, and its revocation by Louis XIV in 1685
The Edict of Saint-Germain, which ended the wars, and its repeal after the famine of the 1600s

options.text: The Peace of Augsburg, which settled a German dispute and was later extended across the Rhine
options.misconception: confuses a French settlement with a German one and reads it as a Rhine treaty

options.text: The Concordat of 1801, which granted a freedom of worship and was suspended in 1790
options.misconception: gives a Church settlement of 1801 the content of a toleration issued two centuries earlier

questions.topic: Centralisation and what it cost
questions.learningObjective: weigh a policy of centralisation against its administrative cost
questions.stem: Under Louis XIV the Crown appoints intendants to the provinces to oversee taxes, justice and public works. What is the trade-off the record shows?

options.text: Stronger control exercised from the capital, paid for by heavier taxation and heavier burdens on the provinces
Weaker control exercised from the capital, since an intendant answers to his own province first
options.misconception: reverses the direction of control, since an intendant is the Crown's man on the spot

options.text: A smaller royal budget, because dues gathered locally cost the Crown less to administer
options.misconception: assumes a uniform system of rules, which is the opposite of what centralisation produced

options.text: A separate administration for each province, since every intendant wrote rules of his own
options.misconception: believes centralising the tax machinery reduced the amount that had to be gathered

The trap is reading a uniform administration as a weak one.

questions.topic: A revolutionary law against workers' combinations
questions.learningObjective: state the social effect of the law of 1791 on collective action
questions.stem: A law passed in 1791 in France forbids workers to combine in guilds and forbids strikes. What social effect did that law have?

options.text: It made collective action illegal for workers, and is cited as the origin of the legal ban on unions
It gave workers the right to organise, since revolutionary legislation favoured every form of freedom
options.misconception: assigns a prohibitory law to a revolution famous for abolishing old prohibitions

options.text: It applied only to the countryside, since towns already had their own separate legal status
options.misconception: reads a decree on association as a measure confined to rural districts

options.text: It fixed wages for a decade, which is what the revolutionary assemblies set out to do
options.misconception: confuses a prohibition with a price control, which is a different measure entirely

The trap is the assumption that revolutionary legislation liberalised everything it touched.

questions.topic: The Encyclopédie and the print culture behind it
questions.learningObjective: identify what the Encyclopédie shows about eighteenth-century print
questions.stem: A multivolume reference work published in France in the second half of the eighteenth century set out to collect human knowledge, with each article written by a named contributor. What does it show?

options.text: That a print culture could organise and license a mass of knowledge, under censorship, for a large public
That printing already existed in France during the Middle Ages and had reached this size by 1400
options.misconception: moves a product of the 1750s back into the fifteenth century, where printing was still scarce

options.text: That a single author spoke alone in the 1700s and that reply was not possible in print
options.misconception: conceives of publication as an act of isolation rather than as an exchange of replies

options.text: That newspapers already carried long articles and reviews in the middle of the fifteenth century
options.misconception: credits the daily press with the form of a reference work produced once, not daily

The trap is treating an encyclopaedia as a solitary book rather than as a coordinated industry.

questions.topic: Why the French Revolution began in 1789
questions.learningObjective: state the immediate cause of the Revolution in 1789
questions.stem: A textbook opens the French Revolution of 1789 with a crisis of the state rather than with a dispute about ideas. What was that crisis?

Religious, so that the Revolution began in a quarrel about the meaning of one sacrament
options.misconception: makes a financial emergency a theological dispute, which is a different history

options.text: Dynastic, so that the whole country fought to place a different family upon the throne
options.misconception: reads a constitutional crisis as a succession war fought over the crown

options.text: Colonial, since the loss of America in 1783 was paid for by a tax the Third Estate refused
options.misconception: puts an eighteenth-century war in the place of the state's own accounts

questions.topic: Abolition and its reversal in the colonies
questions.learningObjective: interpret the sequence of abolition and restoration of slavery
questions.stem: The National Convention abolished slavery in the French colonies in 1794, and the abolition was undone in 1802. What does that sequence show?

options.text: That a legal change could be made and unmade by a few years of politics, while the colony had no say
That slavery had already ended for good in 1794, since a decree of that year was never withdrawn
options.misconception: treats a decree that was in fact repealed as a permanent settlement

options.text: That French law reached the colonies only after 1802 and had no force before that date
options.misconception: dates the reach of metropolitan law to a year set by the restoration of slavery

options.text: That a change of regime in France never reached the colonies in either direction at all
options.misconception: supposes a change of regime leaves the colonies untouched, which the sequence disproves

The trap is reading the first decree as the end of the story.
questions.hint: Ask what the later decree does to the meaning of the earlier one.

questions.topic: The Civil Code of 1804
questions.learningObjective: state the equality the Civil Code established
questions.stem: The Civil Code of 1804 abolished the old legal distinction between the privileged and the ordinary. What equality did it establish?

options.text: Equality before the law between the sons of nobles and the sons of commoners, under a single body of law
Equality of property between men and women, which gave women control of their own goods
options.misconception: attributes to the Code an equality in property that it did not establish for women

options.text: Equality of religion, which made every confession equally official throughout the country
options.misconception: reads a civil code as though it regulated worship across the whole territory

options.text: Equality of political rights, which gave every adult a vote in the assemblies of the Republic
options.misconception: confuses civil standing with the right to vote, which the Code said nothing about

The trap is widening a real reform into one it did not make.

questions.topic: The constitutional laws of 1875
questions.learningObjective: explain what the 1873-1875 constitutional laws settled
questions.stem: After the fall of the Second Empire in 1870, a series of constitutional laws passed between 1873 and 1875 fixed the form of the regime. What were they fixing?

options.text: The republican form of the government, settled by law after a series of votes rather than by one act
The hereditary succession to the throne, so that the new regime kept a king without a crown
options.misconception: reads a republican settlement as one that preserved a throne, which is its opposite

options.text: The right of the colonies to refuse laws, a right each assembly then used against the budget
options.misconception: credits the colonies with a veto that no French constitutional law of the period created

options.text: The abolition of the presidency, leaving the government in the hands of a single assembly
options.misconception: believes the 1875 laws removed the presidency, when the text created a president

questions.explanation: The defeat of 1870 left the form of government open, and the laws of 1873, 1874 and 1875 settled it as a parliamentary republic under a president with limited powers, chosen by the assemblies. Writing it down after a contested vote was deliberate: the lesson of the Second Empire was that an unsettled regime invites an army to settle it. The trap is looking for a restoration, when the whole point of the laws was to close the question.
questions.hint: Ask what the text of 1875 was written to prevent happening again.

questions.learningObjective: interpret the 1884 revision of the constitutional preamble
questions.stem: An amendment inserted into the constitutional preamble in 1884 states that the Republic is a democratic, social and parliamentary regime. What was it defining?

The right of citizens to hold public office, which a preamble of a republic must state first

options.text: The end of elections, since a parliamentary republic is governed in the end by appointment

options.misconception: treats the revision as the completion of a suppression the 1875 laws did not begin

questions.topic: Paying for reconstruction after 1914-1918
questions.learningObjective: explain how post-war reconstruction was funded in France
questions.stem: Northern French towns had to be rebuilt after the war of 1914-1918, and German reparations helped pay for the work. What does that show about the cost of the war?

options.text: That part of the cost fell on the defeated country and was paid out over years after the fighting stopped
That the state had already set aside enough to rebuild and the reparations were a bonus besides
options.misconception: assumes a war left a reserve fund for the damage, which no account of the debts supports

options.text: That German industry rebuilt the towns itself at no cost to anyone and without being asked
options.misconception: credits the victor with an unpaid construction industry, rather than with cash compensation

options.text: That France refused all foreign credit and rebuilt alone entirely at its own expense
options.misconception: reads a mixed financing arrangement as a refusal of all outside help

questions.learningObjective: identify what the Popular Front government changed in 1936
questions.stem: The Popular Front government introduced the forty-hour week and paid leave. Which of these belongs to the same moment?

The end of all strikes, since a government granting leave must also forbid industrial action

options.text: A fixed rate of exchange for the franc, which the Popular Front agreed in return for credit

The years of the war of 1914-1918, when German troops held French towns from 1914 to 1918

questions.learningObjective: explain the failure of the Fourth Republic's governments
questions.stem: Between 1946 and 1958 the Fourth Republic produced short-lived governments, most without a majority in Parliament. What was the result?

questions.learningObjective: explain the function of a fixed exchange rate
questions.stem: Between 1960 and 1971 the French franc was held at a fixed rate against the dollar under the system set up at Bretton Woods. What does a fixed rate do?

options.text: It fixes the price of one currency in another, so an importer or exporter can price without guessing
It fixes the price of goods inside the country, since one rate would then apply to every article
options.misconception: confuses an external rate between two currencies with an internal price list

options.text: It raises the value of the currency at home, because a fixed rate is taken to promise a strong coin
options.misconception: reads monetary stability as a claim about the strength of the currency rather than about its price

That the body had been abolished in 1614 and was restored by a later law before meeting in 1789
options.misconception: converts an absence into an abolition, which is a different kind of interruption

options.text: That the body met regularly until 1614 and then stopped while the country was reforming itself
options.misconception: credits the body with a regular existence that the statement explicitly denies

options.text: That the assembly of 1614 was the first of its kind, and that 1789 was its successor some decades on
options.misconception: reverses the direction of time, making 1789 a development of 1614 rather than a revival

questions.explanation: The Estates-General, a representative body of the three orders, was last summoned in 1614 and was summoned again in May 1789, which is what made the meeting so extraordinary and so difficult to run. questions.subject: FRENCH
questions.topic: A method for dating an unknown document
questions.learningObjective: describe a method for dating a document from internal and external evidence
questions.stem: Explain the method you would teach a learner for dating a document of unknown origin, and show it on a charter that carries a seal and no date.

answer.exemplar: Two families of evidence, and the learner should be told which one comes first. External evidence comes first, because it is the more reliable: a seal identifies a person and a territory, a notarial register identifies a notary whose activity is dated, a coin struck under a known ruler places the document between two events, and a watermark identifies the paper. Internal evidence comes second, because it is a claim the document makes about itself: a regnal year, a reference to an event, a computus, an indulgence naming a jubilee. Only after both is a date proposed, and it should be proposed as a range with a reason. Applied to a charter with a seal and no written date: the seal gives an authority, the authority's tenure is established from other charters bearing the same seal, and the intersection of that tenure with anything the text mentions is the dating range. A document is then said to be dated by the day of the month it carries, with the year supplied externally, which is why a lost seal leaves a text undated rather than merely uncertain.

questions.explanation: The order is the method, and it is the opposite of the order most people try, since a date written on a page is the first thing the eye looks for. External evidence is stronger because it is not produced by the same hand as the claim, which is the only advantage that matters when a document may be a forgery. The method is also falsifiable, since each step names the document that would confirm or break it. What to watch is the reflex of the confident single date, which is almost always two plausible dates presented as one.
questions.hint: Ask which of the two families of evidence is produced by somebody other than the document's writer.

questions.subject: FRENCH
questions.topic: A method for reading a primary source
questions.learningObjective: describe a method for establishing what a primary source can prove
questions.stem: Explain the method you would teach a learner for reading a primary source, and show it on a royal ordinance that announces new duties on the towns.

answer.exemplar: Four questions, asked before the document is believed. First, who wrote it, for whom, and with what interest, because a document is a position and not a window. Second, when it was written, since a law changes meaning once the situation that produced it has changed, and a rule announced in an emergency is read differently from the same rule announced in a stable year. Third, what the document is for, and a law is not for describing the world but for requiring something, which means its sentences state intentions rather than measurements. Fourth, what corroborating material exists, which is accounts, court records and the repeated reissue of rules that were not obeyed. Applied to the ordinance: it is strong evidence that the Crown intended the duties, and it is no evidence at all that the towns paid them, and the way to find out is to look for the accounts. The learner who stops at the third question has a document that cannot be wrong about its own intention and tells them nothing else.

questions.explanation: The method works because it separates what a document knows from what it asserts, and a law sits at the far end of the assertiveness scale. Each question can be answered with evidence rather than with opinion, which is what makes the method teachable. The fourth question is the one that turns a reading into a piece of history, since a rule that was not applied is itself a finding. What to watch is treating a document as transparent, which is the assumption the whole method exists to remove.
questions.hint: Ask what the ordinance is evidence of, and of what it is not evidence of.

questions.subject: FRENCH
questions.topic: A method for testing a generalisation about a century
questions.learningObjective: describe a method for testing a claim made about a whole period
questions.stem: Explain the method you would teach a learner for testing a claim that an entire century had one character, and show it on the claim that the eighteenth century in France was one of plain religious decline.

answer.exemplar: Three steps, in this order. Break the claim into parts it must satisfy: if a century is uniformly one thing, then the direction of change should be the same at the beginning, in the middle and at the end, and any reversal is a counter-example. Then go looking for the reversal, and look for it in the records of ordinary life rather than in the statements of institutions, since a claim about belief is best tested against registers, accounts and the volume of work commissioned. Then state the claim in a form the evidence can support, which usually means something about direction and about the balance of forces rather than about disappearance. Applied to the claim: the loss of the Church's jurisdiction to the parlements is a real and documented change, but a century in which religious practice ends is a claim the parish registers of the decades after 1789 do not bear out, and an argument about authority is not an argument about belief. The claim survives in a weaker form, and the weaker form is the one worth writing down.

questions.explanation: The method works because a claim about a period is always a claim about direction, and direction is falsifiable by a single well-chosen document. Step two is the difficult one, since a counter-example is usually found in a register rather than in the history book that made the claim. Step three is what keeps the exercise honest, because a reformulated claim is one a reader can check. What to watch is the strong form, which sounds like a summary and behaves like an assertion nobody has tested.
questions.hint: Ask what single document would be enough to break a claim about a whole century.

questions.subject: FRENCH
questions.topic: A method for explaining a constitutional change
questions.learningObjective: describe a method for explaining a change of regime without reducing it to dates
questions.stem: Explain the method you would teach a learner for explaining a change of constitution in France, and show it on the replacement of the parliamentary republic of the 1875 laws by the constitution of 1958.

answer.exemplar: Four questions, asked of any change of constitution. First, what problem was the earlier arrangement failing to solve, since no constitution is written in the absence of a difficulty, and the difficulty is what gives the change its meaning. Second, what was kept, which is usually most of it, and naming what survived is what stops a change being described as a clean break. Third, where the initiative came from and how it was settled, whether by an assembly, a negotiation or a transfer of powers under pressure, since the route explains the fragility of the result. Fourth, what the new text was meant to make impossible, which is the only question that turns a list of articles into an argument. Applied to 1958: the parliamentary arithmetic of the Fourth Republic had produced governments that could not survive long enough to conduct a war; much of the 1958 text is the republic of 1875 with the government made durable; the settlement came after a crisis in which full powers were returned to a single man; and the article on emergency powers exists so that no future assembly will again be unable to act. Every point is checkable against the two texts.

questions.explanation: The method works because it forces the comparison to be made between texts rather than between slogans, and a text is something anybody can open. The fourth question is what makes an explanation teachable, because it connects an article to a fear. The trap is the summary that says a country became more democratic or more stable, which is neither true nor false until it is attached to a paragraph. What to watch is the fifth question nobody asks, which is what the change cost.
questions.hint: Ask which question turns a list of articles into an argument.

questions.subject: FRENCH
questions.topic: A method for weighing two rival explanations
questions.learningObjective: describe a method for comparing two explanations of the same change
questions.stem: Explain the method you would teach a learner for choosing between two explanations of the same historical change, and show it on whether the collapse of a monarchy was caused by the financial crisis or by the loss of a war.

answer.exemplar: Three tests, applied in this order. The scope test: a cause must be able to explain the timing, so the explanation is compared with a chronology, and a cause that was present for thirty years without producing the change has not explained anything about the year it happened. The asymmetry test: if one explanation requires the other to be false, the pair is not competing, and the argument has to be reformulated before it can be tested. The counter-case test: each explanation is applied to a case where it should have produced the change and did not, or produced it later than expected, and the surviving explanation is the one whose predictions hold. Applied to the two explanations: the financial crisis is present for years before the political rupture, which weakens it as a cause of timing, while the loss of a war and the events that followed it are both recent and decisive; and a monarchy with a functioning tax system survives a long war, which suggests the crisis is doing the necessary work and the war the triggering work. Neither is the whole, and the method says so rather than choosing.

questions.explanation: The three tests are the standard way of turning a debate into a research programme, and the third is the one that does the work, because a cause that cannot fail is not a cause. The first test is cheap and is skipped most often, and skipping it is how a long-standing grievance is later credited with a short revolution. The method is teachable because each test asks for a document or a date. What to watch is the third-party interest in the debate, since an explanation that flatters one region, one class or one institution will pass the asymmetry test and fail the third.
questions.hint: Ask which of the three tests can be run with a calendar and no reading at all.

questions.subject: FRENCH
questions.topic: A method for checking a claim against a collection
questions.learningObjective: describe a method for testing a claim against museum and archival evidence
questions.stem: Explain the method you would teach a learner for checking a claim about a period against a museum collection, and show it on a claim that a painter's series of the 1890s shows a growing interest in light.

answer.exemplar: Four steps, in this order. State the claim as something countable, because a claim about interest is checked by counting works and a claim about feeling is not checked at all. Establish what the collection contains and what it cannot contain, since a museum holds what was preserved, bought or bequeathed, and absence from a collection is not absence from the period. Compare the count across periods rather than across artists, so that a change in the practice of the whole art world shows up in the numbers. And separate the production of the work from its survival, since a series that was painted and then dispersed is evidence of a practice in its own time and not of what a later public saw. Applied to the claim: the series of haystacks and of the Rouen cathedral recorded in French public collections between 1890 and 1900 is counted and dated, and the count is compared with the previous decade and with the collections of other countries, which is what would show whether the interest was general or peculiar to one dealer. The verdict will be about the surviving record, which is the only thing a collection can speak to.

questions.explanation: The method works because it replaces an impression with a count, and because it asks in advance what the evidence is capable of answering. Step two is where most claims fail, since a collection is a selection made under conditions nobody would have chosen. Step four protects against a common error, which is reading a museum's arrangement as though it were the period's arrangement. What to watch is the temptation to use the catalogue as a list of masterpieces and stop counting.
questions.hint: Ask what a collection can tell you about what people bought, and about what was made.

The private income of a rural family in 1840, of which no series of figures survives in any archive

options.misconception: takes an official statement as a description of practice, which is the error the study exists to catch

The fonds and the series that could hold the answer are found, and the dates of the series noted

The answer is written with its limits stated, so that a later reader can see what was not established

questions.subject: FRENCH
questions.topic: A claim that the Terror ended the Revolution
questions.learningObjective: correct a periodisation claim in two stages
questions.stem: Stage one: a pupil writes « the Terror ended the Revolution ». Say what is wrong with the sentence as history. Stage two: say what the record does show about the years that follow.

answer.exemplar: Stage one: the sentence uses a moral adjective as a boundary, and a boundary cannot be a feeling. The Terror is a name for a phase with institutions and measures — a committee of public safety, tribunals that judged without the ordinary delays, and price controls — and what ended it was a decision about those measures, not a change of mood. The sentence also leaves the period unnamed on the far side, so the reader is not told what the pupil thinks came next, and a claim that erases a decade cannot be checked against anything. The correction is to replace the adjective with a date and an institution: the emergency government of 1793 and 1794, closed by the fall of Robespierre in the summer of 1794. Stage two: what the record shows is that the revolution did not stop, it changed constitution. A new constitution followed in 1795, the executive was placed in a council of directors, and the decade closed with the coup of the eighteenth of Brumaire in 1799, which produced a settled regime and a lasting rearrangement of the executive. So the accurate sentence is that the Terror was the most intense phase of a revolution that continued, and the strongest evidence for that is constitutional: texts were being written, agreed and then replaced, which is what a revolution still in progress looks like from a later distance.

questions.explanation: The two stages are separated because a correction and a replacement are different operations, and a pupil who is only corrected will simply choose a new adjective. Naming the measures in the first stage and naming the constitution in the second turns a moral judgement into a chronology, which is the only form in which such a claim can be argued about. What to watch is the habit of treating a familiar label as a period, when it is a label.
questions.hint: Ask which institution the pupil has mistaken for a boundary.

The trap is the compression that sounds complete because it names a real fact and connects it to a real book.

answer.exemplar: Stage one: the historian may claim only what is visible from outside the closed file, which means the series it belongs to, its dates, its volume in the finding aid, and whatever earlier restrictions or partial openings have already revealed about its contents. Any statement about what the closed documents say is, for now, an inference from the series rather than a reading, and it should be written as one. Stage two: the historian may not claim that the file contains what a finding aid's title suggests, that its silence proves anything, or that a conclusion drawn from neighbouring files holds for it. The wording of the conclusion should therefore change in three ways: the verb of evidence moves from shows to suggests, the date of the conclusion is stated, and the document that would settle the question is named. So the sentence becomes that on the basis of the neighbouring series, and subject to the file being opened in the year of its release, the practice in this office appears to have been such and such. What to watch is the drift in which an inference acquires the grammar of a finding, and is then cited by somebody else as a reading.

questions.explanation: The two stages are separated because the second is where the real damage is done: a claim about a closed file is not a weaker claim, it is a different kind of claim, and it must be written in different words. Naming the document that would settle the question is what makes the limitation productive, since it tells the next reader exactly where to go. What to watch is the habit of citing a finding aid as though it were a document.

questions.subject: FRENCH
questions.topic: Two rival dates for one charter
questions.learningObjective: resolve a dating disagreement in two stages
questions.stem: Stage one: two specialists date the same charter differently, one from the regnal year named in the text and one from the notary's seal. Say which evidence should carry the more weight and why. Stage two: say how you would write the date in a note so that a later reader can check the disagreement.

answer.exemplar: Stage one: the seal carries the more weight, because it is external evidence and the regnal year is a claim made inside the document by the party who wrote it. A regnal year can be a slip, a copyist's error or a deliberate misdating, and a forgery is built precisely out of an internal date that looks right. The seal identifies a person and a notary's register, and a notary's activity is bounded by documents that are independently dated, so the intersection of those dates is evidence the document did not choose. The regnal year is not discarded: it is retained as a check, and where the two disagree the disagreement itself becomes a finding about the text, usually a copy of an earlier act. Stage two: the note states both dates, the evidence behind each, and the reason for preferring one, and it gives the range within which the act falls rather than a single year. So the note reads that the act is dated by the regnal year to 1387 and by the notary's register to 1384, the discrepancy suggesting a later copy of an act of 1384, and the reference used throughout is the register. A later reader then has the three things needed to disagree, which a single confident year does not provide.

questions.explanation: The two stages are separated because the first is a judgement about evidence and the second is a piece of technical writing that makes the judgement checkable. The preference for external evidence is the standard of the discipline, and its cost should be stated rather than hidden, since an internally consistent reign can occasionally be better evidence than a misattributed seal. What to watch is the pressure to publish a single date, which reads as confidence and is actually the loss of the argument.
